analysis.one_liner: Shields companies supplying raw materials and parts for medical implants from product-liability lawsuits by injured patients.
analysis.headline: Backed by 26 senators from both parties, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies that sell generic raw materials and component parts to implant makers were being dragged into lawsuits over devices they never designed or tested. This bill would have let those suppliers get out of such lawsuits almost automatically: a judge could dismiss them based only on paperwork, patients could not gather evidence while the motion was pending, patients who sued a supplier would have to name the implant maker instead, and patients who lost could be ordered to pay the supplier's legal fees. It also excluded claims about silicone gel breast implants entirely. Supporters said this was needed to keep materials flowing to lifesaving implants; the practical effect was to move the cost of implant injuries away from suppliers and onto patients and device makers.
analysis.who_benefits: Suppliers of raw materials and component parts used in implants (things like silicones, metals, and polymers that are also sold for non-medical uses) would gain the most. They could escape lawsuits from injured patients with a quick dismissal on written affidavits, face no evidence-gathering while the motion was decided, and collect attorney fees if a court found the claim frivolous. Medical device manufacturers would gain a more reliable supply chain, since the bill's own findings state that litigation costs had driven some suppliers to stop selling into the medical market. People who need implants would benefit only indirectly, through continued availability of materials — an outcome the bill itself argued for but never demonstrated with evidence of actual device shortages.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Raw-material and parts suppliers to implant makers

how_it_helps.text: A supplier could file a motion to dismiss a lawsuit against it, and the court would rule based only on the parties' pleadings and affidavits — with no discovery allowed until the motion was decided [S3].

A supplier would be liable only if it actually manufactured the implant, held title to it as a seller, or delivered materials that failed to meet contractual specifications — otherwise it would be excluded from liability entirely [S3].
A claimant who named a supplier and lost on a finding that the claim was frivolous would have to pay the supplier's attorney fees and costs [S3].

The bill's findings state that suppliers had ceased supplying certain materials because litigation costs exceeded their small medical-market sales, and that foreign suppliers were refusing to sell into the U.S. market [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People harmed by implants would bear the cost. They could generally pursue only the implant manufacturer or a seller holding title, not the materials suppliers; the manufacturer would have to be named as a party; the case against a supplier could be thrown out on affidavits without any opportunity to gather evidence; and an unsuccessful claimant risked paying the supplier's legal fees. Claims arising from silicone gel and the silicone envelope in breast implants would be excluded from the act's protections entirely, and that exclusion could not be disclosed to a jury. State laws giving patients stronger remedies would be superseded where the bill sets a rule.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients injured by implanted medical devices

drawbacks.text: A patient suing a supplier would face dismissal based on paperwork alone, with no discovery permitted until the court ruled — making it far harder to build a case against a company that had actual knowledge of the materials' behavior [S3].
Requiring claimants who lose to pay a supplier's attorney fees would deter many valid, hard-to-prove claims, not just frivolous ones [S3].

The bill excluded silicone gel breast implant claims from its definition of claimant while barring that exclusion from being disclosed to a jury — a targeted carve-out that appears to respond to the wave of breast-implant litigation of the 1990s [S3].

Supporters' own argument — that suppliers were exiting the market and devices would become unavailable — was asserted in the bill's findings, and the bill offered no independent mechanism, such as a compensation fund, to make injured patients whole if suppliers escaped liability [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There was a real problem behind this bill: courts were rarely holding suppliers liable, but defending even weak claims cost more than the suppliers earned from the tiny medical market, and some stopped selling into it. The bill addressed that by essentially immunizing suppliers and shifting the burden of implant injuries onto patients and implant makers. It offered injured people nothing in return — no alternative compensation path — and its mandatory fee-shifting and no-discovery dismissal procedure went well beyond simply codifying the common court finding that suppliers have no duty to warn. The availability argument was plausible but unproven, and the silicone breast implant carve-out suggests the bill was aimed as much at one active litigation problem as at the general supply issue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee in February 1997, but the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 26, 1997 by Senator Lieberman with seven original cosponsors and was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
It drew 25 cosponsors — 22 Republicans and 3 Democrats — including the Senate Majority Leader [S4].
No further action appears in the record: the committee never reported the bill, and the Senate never debated or voted on it before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients injured by implants, and the plaintiff lawyers who represent them, were better off because the bill died: suppliers remain subject to the same state-law liability rules as before, with no added dismissal procedures or fee-shifting. Biomaterials suppliers remain exposed to the litigation costs that prompted the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — a Democratic sponsor, 22 Republican and 3 Democratic cosponsors including the Republican Majority Leader — and no recorded opposition ever appeared, because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would nearly immunize these suppliers from lawsuits by people harmed by implants, allowing dismissal on affidavits with no discovery, plus fee-shifting against losing claimants. Their gain is a direct reduction in injured patients' legal remedies.

The bill excludes claims about silicone gel and silicone envelopes in breast implants from its scope and bars disclosing that exclusion to a jury — a carve-out aimed squarely at the era's breast-implant litigation.

Device makers would gain a steadier supply of materials, which the bill argues had been choked off by litigation risk. But the bill requires claimants to name the implant manufacturer as a party, concentrating liability on them instead.

Mandatory dismissal procedures, no discovery during motions, and mandatory attorney-fee awards for frivolous claims would sharply reduce the number of implant-injury cases lawyers could bring against suppliers.
